meta.title: Bug Hunt Bench
meta.subtitle: 105 real bugs hidden in two production repos. Frontier coding models find and fix what they can, graded blind.
meta.author: Pawel Huryn

method: Two unrelated production codebases: a ~28K-line TypeScript VS Code extension (45 bugs) and a ~60K-line React/Supabase LMS (60 bugs). Most bugs are real regressions reverted from the repos' own fix history, each with its fix commit.
The test suites stay green, so nothing points at the answers. Every model gets the identical prompt, one round per repo, in its own native agentic CLI.
Grading is blind: the model's diff is the ground truth, not its report. An independent judge scores against a withheld answer key and never learns which model produced the diff.

The score counts planted bugs only. Some models bug-max - they report a long list of real but irrelevant problems, and that list has no answer key and no ceiling, so counting it would just reward volume. Unplanted fixes are tracked separately and never scored.

glossary.fixed: Planted bugs fixed and verified against the withheld answer key. The only number in the score.
glossary.partial: The defect was addressed but not fully closed. Not counted in the score.
glossary.claimed_only: Named in the model's report but not fixed in its diff - including bugs it saw and chose not to touch. Not counted in the score.
glossary.extras: A real defect the model fixed that nobody planted. Genuine work - but the set has no answer key and no ceiling, so it cannot be scored reliably. Counted, never added to the score.
glossary.cost_bill: An actual invoice or credits delta.
glossary.cost_list: A token-count estimate at published list rates, not a bill.
glossary.cost_floor: Reconstructed lower bound - this CLI reports context occupancy, not billing.
glossary.cost_free: Served free at the time of the run.
glossary.effort_verified_ceiling: This model's highest reasoning setting. We checked that changing the setting actually changes what the model does.
glossary.effort_verified: We checked that changing this reasoning setting actually changes what the model does.
glossary.effort_first_party: A setting the vendor documents in their own tool. Taken at face value, not separately tested.
glossary.effort_clamped: We asked for a higher setting and the tool quietly ran a lower one. Published as a correction.
glossary.effort_inert_default: This route ignores the effort setting entirely, so the model ran at its own default. There was no working dial to turn.

caveats: One round per model per repo. Same-setting variance is real and measured: three Grok 4.5 runs on identical settings scored 16, 13 and 17.

Wall clock is the same measure on every row: repo 1 plus repo 2 agent time, with dependency install and health checks excluded. Two things bend it, and both are marked on the score-and-time map. Three runs took their two repo legs concurrently - the sum is still like-for-like, but two agents sharing one machine and one API key contend, so those figures can run high rather than low. And one figure is adjusted: the retired-Gemini-CLI run excludes a 35-minute harness stall, the only number here that is not what the harness measured.

Cost is not one kind of number: some figures are an actual bill, some are a token-count estimate at published list rates, one CLI only allows a reconstructed lower bound, and one run was free. The key under the board names which is which - they are not interchangeable, and none of them is a quote for what you would pay.
39 of the 105 bugs have survived every model in every run to date. The count moves as new runs land: it fell from 49 to 44 during the 27-28 August waves.

runs.caveat: Mixed judges within this row: repo 1 by GPT-5.5, repo 2 by Grok 4.5 after the Codex judge returned a malformed verdict on that packet. Every other Fable 5.1 row is Codex-judged throughout. The repo 2 leg was also re-run: the first attempt spanned a network outage that voided its wall clock (862 vs 2183 output tokens/min) and scored 18/60 under Codex, against 16/60 under Grok here. The diff and the judge both changed between those two, so the difference cannot be attributed to either one.

One run per tier, five tiers - so this is five samples describing a surface, not a measured response curve. The board's own variance evidence (three runs of one model at one setting scoring 16, 13 and 17) means a twelve-point spread across four single runs is entirely consistent with noise, which is precisely the point: if noise can produce this ordering, the ordering carries no information. The one claim that survives is max against the rest, and even that rests on a single run at each end.
runs.note: The row that completes Fable 5.1's dial, and the one that shows the dial does not behave. All five tiers now exist at one run each: low 29, medium 21, high 33, xhigh 29, max 43. The four below max span twelve points in no order whatsoever - xhigh lands BELOW high and exactly level with low, medium is the worst of the five - while max sits ten clear above the best of them. The run itself is clean: both legs exited success with a report written, 13/45 on repo 1 and 16/60 on repo 2. So the honest reading of this model's effort control is that only the top of it is doing visible work on this benchmark; between low and xhigh the label does not predict the score. That matters because the effort column is the thing readers most often take as an ordering, and here it is not one.

runs.caveat: One run at this tier. The effort ceiling is real but flat: the same probe shows high (9946-14061), xhigh (8266-19309) and max (6542-14902) are mutually indistinguishable with means that fall as the nominal tier rises, so max is the top of the dial and buys nothing measurable over high - the same two-rung shape the Qwen3.8-Flash probe found, which suggests it is a property of Alibaba's serving rather than of either model. Note also that this endpoint's accept-list CONTRADICTS the QwenCloud doc the superseded row relied on (low|medium|xhigh with high->xhigh), which is one more reason that row's tier claim was never safe. Cost is a list-price ESTIMATE and not a bill - DashScope exposes no credits API on this path - computed from the run's own token counts at 2.00 in / 2.50 cache-write / 0.25 cache-read / 6.00 out per MTok, from OpenRouter's Alibaba-endpoint listing. Finally, do NOT read the 9-point gain as caused by the path. It is n=1 against n=1 and almost all of it is one repo - repo 1 went 5/45 to 13/45 while repo 2 moved by one - and this board has seen the same model at the same setting swing 6 points on repo 1 (Opus 5 at medium: 11/8/14). A systematic path effect should have moved both repos and did not, so the score difference is unexplained and may simply be variance. What the pair DOES establish beyond variance is the cost and token behaviour, where the gap is ~5,000x and not a coin flip.
runs.note: The Aug 3 Qwen3.8-Max row re-run on Alibaba's OWN Anthropic-compatible endpoint - no local proxy, no aggregator - and it is the clearest demonstration on this board that a row records a SERVING PATH and not just a model. Same model, same harness, same two repos, same laptop, one hop removed: 28/105 against 19/105, 103.4 min against 148.1, $26.29 against $33.30. Nine points more for a fifth less money and a third less time, and the gain is concentrated in repo 1, which went 5/45 to 13/45. The mechanism is visible in the token columns. The OpenRouter run billed 12.94% of its prompt tokens as UNCACHED INPUT - 8,282,777 of them, $16.57, half that row's cost - while this one billed 0.0019%, or 1,716 tokens across both legs. Caching that keeps working means the model keeps its context instead of rebuilding it, which is why output ROSE 23% (168,395 tokens against 136,426) while wall time FELL: it did more thinking and less re-reading. Effort here is measured, not requested - the endpoint 400-rejects an invented tier and names its accept-list (low, medium, high, xhigh, max), and an n=3-per-tier probe on this exact path separates the bottom of the dial cleanly (mean output tokens low=4495 against high=12422, low's range overlapping none of the top three, 3.09x between-tier ratio against a 2.34x worst within-tier spread). 28 strict matches, 2 partials, 3 claimed-only, 6 genuine unplanted extras.
Sequential re-run of the 08-12 concurrent-legs xhigh - both scored 27/105 (n=2 agreement), and this one has a comparable single-machine wall, so it replaces the dotted original.

runs.caveat: One run at this tier, and repo 1 is a RETRY. The first repo-1 attempt at this exact setting made 70 successful tool calls across 73 turns with zero permission denials, then wrote 'Let me check a few remaining details before fixing...' and ended its turn having written no report - a healthy environment and a model that narrated its next step instead of taking it. The retry delivered 13/45 in 42.5 minutes, so that was a fluke rather than a property, but a top-effort run that silently stops on one repo in two attempts is itself a reliability signal, and the published wall and cost figures cover the retry only. Cost is a list-price ESTIMATE and not a bill - DashScope exposes no credits API on this path - computed from the run's own token counts at 0.15 in / 0.20 cache-write / 0.016 cache-read / 0.47 out per MTok. Do not read this row as a ceiling for the Qwen 3.8 family: it is the ceiling of the SMALL model. The Qwen3.8-Max row on this board ran a different path entirely (Claude Code -> local proxy -> OpenRouter) and is not a clean comparison.
runs.note: The top of Alibaba's own accept-list on Alibaba's own Anthropic-compatible endpoint - no aggregator, no local proxy. 26/105 for $1.81 at list. Read it against its low companion, which is the point of running both: max buys THREE points over low (23/105) for 32% more money and the same wall clock (97.3 min against 98.1). The effort label is measured rather than requested - the endpoint 400-rejects an invented tier and names its accept-list (low, medium, high, xhigh, max), and an n=3-per-tier magnitude probe on this exact path shows the dial binds at the bottom: mean output tokens run low=3557, medium=4579, high=19329, and the 5.43x spread between lowest and highest mean clears the worst within-tier spread of 2.00x. So max is the real ceiling of a real dial. What it is NOT is a fifth rung: high (13933-27933), xhigh (12523-24778) and max (13767-19431) overlap almost entirely and their means FALL as the nominal tier rises, so paying for max over high buys nothing measurable. 26 strict matches, 3 partials, 3 claimed-only, 7 genuine unplanted extras.
The Opus dial is nearly flat at the top: high 21, medium 24, xhigh 26, max 27.

runs.caveat: The endpoint deserializer also accepts an undocumented `ultra`, which DeepSeek own docs never mention (they give none|low|high|max, default high). Sampled n=4 it straddles both high and max and resolves to neither, and nothing in that sample exceeds max band - so `max` is the top of the documented dial and nothing measured reasons more than it, which is what the ceiling label claims. Which tier `ultra` aliases is unresolved and left that way rather than guessed.
runs.note: DeepSeek newest Flash generation, benchmarked on DeepSeek OWN Anthropic-compatible API - no aggregator, no proxy. Claude Code puts --effort on the wire as output_config.effort; the endpoint 400-rejects an invented tier and names its enum, and a thinking-volume sweep separates the tiers with DISJOINT ranges (high mean 30.5K chars, max mean 83.6K, n=3), so max was applied and not merely requested. Cost is a real bill, not an estimate: DeepSeek sells prepaid credit, so each leg is charged at the balance drop across it. $1.08 of real credit for 24/105 - the same score as Fable 5 and as Opus 5 at medium. Those two are list estimates and this is a bill, so read the gap as an order of magnitude and not as a ratio.

runs.caveat: One run at this tier. More importantly, read this row with its max companion rather than as the bottom rung of a working ladder: the same probe shows the dial SATURATES above low, with high, xhigh and max mutually indistinguishable (ranges 13933-27933, 12523-24778 and 13767-19431, means falling as the nominal tier rises). So the honest picture of this model's effort control is two settings, not five. Cost is a list-price ESTIMATE and not a bill - DashScope exposes no credits API on this path - computed from the run's own token counts at 0.15 in / 0.20 cache-write / 0.016 cache-read / 0.47 out per MTok, rates cross-checked against OpenRouter's Alibaba-endpoint listing, which matches Alibaba's published rates exactly on the Qwen3.8-Max row this board already carries.
runs.note: The board's first Qwen row that does not go through an aggregator: Claude Code straight onto Alibaba's own Anthropic-compatible endpoint, no local proxy and no OpenRouter in the path. 23/105 for $1.37 at list puts it between the two DeepSeek V4.1 Flash rows (19/105 at $0.31 and 24/105 at $1.08) and above models costing twenty times more. The effort label here is MEASURED, not merely requested, which is unusual for a cheap model on this board: the endpoint 400-rejects an invented tier and names its accept-list (low, medium, high, xhigh, max), and a magnitude probe at n=3 per tier separates the bottom of the dial cleanly - mean output tokens run low=3557 against high=19329, low and medium sit in bands that do not overlap the top three, and the 5.43x spread between lowest and highest mean clears the worst within-tier spread of 2.00x. So low is a real setting on this path rather than a word in a column. The honesty profile is among the better ones here: 23 strict matches, ZERO partials, only 3 claimed-only across both repos, and 7 genuine unplanted extras.

One run per tier. A single non-monotonic point is a finding about this run, not a demonstrated property of the medium tier - the board's own variance evidence (three Grok 4.5 runs at one setting scoring 16, 13 and 17) is the reason that distinction is enforced here. What the row does establish is that the shell-first strategy and the low score arrived together, which is a mechanism worth having on record either way.
runs.note: Fable 5.1's dial does not run in a straight line: medium scores 21/105, BELOW its own low row (29) and well below high (33) and max (43). The run is clean - both legs exited success, no truncation, no permission denials, no tool errors - and the raw captures say why in the tool mix rather than in the thinking. At medium the model worked almost entirely through the shell: 83 Bash calls against 3 Reads and ZERO Edits or Greps on repo 1, and 99 Bash against 2 Reads and zero Edits on repo 2. At low it read the codebase instead - 44 Reads, 20 Greps, 16 Edits on repo 1. That shows up in the billing shape too: medium pulled 4.0M cached-read tokens on repo 1 against low's 19.7M, because a session that never reads files into context keeps a small context to re-send. Fewer bugs found is what you would expect from a model that barely looked at the code.

runs.caveat: The honesty profile is worse at this tier than at max, which is the opposite of the usual direction: 3 partials and 2 claimed-only here against 0 and 0 at max. At n=1 per tier that is a difference of a handful of bugs, not a demonstrated property of the tier.
runs.note: The dial companion to the max row: same model, same first-party endpoint, same day, one tier down. It costs 5 strict fixes (19/105 against 24) and every one of them is on repo 1 - 9/45 against 14/45, while repo 2 lands on exactly the same 10/60. The tier is doing visibly less work for that: 26.1 min against 42.6, 160K output tokens against 240K, 57M cached reads against 82M, $0.31 against $1.08. high is DeepSeek's documented default, but it is requested explicitly here rather than left implicit, because on this endpoint the omitted field measured as neither high nor max.

runs.caveat: One run on each side of the comparison. Two single runs landing on the same total is not a demonstration that the paths are equivalent - the board has watched one model at one setting score 16, 13 and 17 - and the matching totals here are best read as 'no effect large enough for one run to see' rather than 'no effect'. The wall and cost gaps are the more robust half of this row, because they do not depend on the judge. This arm also ran twice: the first attempt died at 120 turns when the Z.ai balance ran out, and that leg was voided rather than scored. The figures here are the complete re-run.
runs.note: GLM-5.3 on Z.ai's own API at max effort scores 19/105 - the identical total to the board's existing GLM-5.3 row, which ran through OpenRouter at an inert default effort. The splits differ slightly (9/45 + 10/60 here against 8/45 + 11/60 there) and the total does not. Two variables moved between those two rows at once, the serving path AND the requested tier, and neither shifted the score. What did shift is everything else: 40.4 minutes against 66.7, and $15.93 against $19.73. So the first-party route is 1.65x faster and cheaper for the same result. On the tier itself: Z.ai's endpoint 400-rejects an invented effort value and names its accept-list (none, minimal, low, medium, high, xhigh, max), so unlike an aggregator that shrugs and returns 200, this route demonstrably READ the field - but a field being read is not the same as a dial being turned, and no magnitude probe was run here, so this row claims an accepted tier and not a measured one.

The Sep 10 row runs the same model on Z.ai's own API with the tier asserted against an endpoint that rejects invented tiers, scores the same 19/105, and does it in 40.4 min for $15.93 against 66.7 min and $19.73 - so the first-party row replaces this one.

runs.note: CORRECTED 2026-09-12 (4): EFFORT IS INERT ON THIS ROW, measured at last. It shipped verified_ceiling, was corrected to first_party on 09-11, and is now inert_default with effort 'default' - the same label every other aggregator-routed row on this board carries. A nine-runs-per-condition probe on the exact surface this arm used (OpenRouter's Anthropic-compatible /v1/messages, receipts results/effort-dial-probes/20260912-qwen38max-openrouter-anthropic.txt and 20260912-qwen38max-all-n9.txt) puts reasoning.effort=low at mean 13,017 output tokens (7,897-16,402), reasoning.effort=high at 14,815 (11,524-20,237), and NO effort field at all at 13,622 (9,179-19,757) - a 1.14x spread between the tiers against a 2.15x worst within-condition spread, with every range overlapping every other. The field does nothing; the run sat at Alibaba's own default either way. SELF-CORRECTION, same day: for a few hours this note also said the shim had caused the problem by deleting Anthropic's native 'thinking' field to install 'reasoning.effort', on the strength of that field measuring very differently (mean 5,468). That rested on ONE budget value, which can only show a field is read, not that it binds. A three-value probe (receipt results/effort-dial-probes/20260912-qwen38max-budget-scaling-openrouter.txt, n=3 each) put budget_tokens=2,000 at mean 5,627 output tokens, 8,000 at 4,735 and 24,000 at 4,111 - twelve times the budget moved the mean 0.73x, the wrong way, inside a 1.95x worst within-condition spread. So budget_tokens is a switch rather than a dial on this path, and the switch SUPPRESSES: sending it in any form costs about two thirds of the model's thinking against the 13,622 no-field baseline. That makes the shim's pop the configuration producing the MOST thinking available here, not a discarded control - with 'thinking' gone and reasoning.effort inert, the request fell through to the endpoint default, which is exactly what inert_default records. The label is unaffected; only the causal story changed, and the shims were reverted to dropping the field. A control on Alibaba's own endpoint shows native thinking landing far higher there and fully overlapping Alibaba's own no-field baseline, so the suppression is a property of the aggregator hop and not of the model. RE-MEASURED AT n=6 AND THEN n=9 the same day, because a claim this size should not rest on three samples (receipt results/effort-dial-probes/20260912-qwen38max-all-n9.txt, 24 fresh concurrent calls pooled with the originals and the n=6 top-ups; every condition on both routes now stands at nine runs, so no verdict rests on a smaller sample than the one it is compared against): through OpenRouter budget_tokens=24,000 gives mean 4,967 (3,568-7,637) against a no-field baseline of 13,622 (9,179-19,757); straight to Alibaba the same field gives 13,168 (9,185-15,977) against 14,379 (11,586-17,442). All verdicts survive - cross-route 2.65x against a 2.15x worst within-cell spread, ranges disjoint, the field costing 64% of the thinking through the hop and nothing at all direct. The effort WORD reads more inert at nine runs than at three: low-vs-high means 1.14x through OpenRouter and 1.04x direct, ranges fully overlapping. The bigger samples did move one number: the OpenRouter no-field baseline measured 15,714 at n=3, 13,339 at n=6 and 13,622 at n=9 - three samples had overestimated it by 15%, and the six- and nine-run readings agree to 2%. Quote the nine-run figures only. Ranges can only widen with n, so each pass was a test the finding could fail. Still at n=3 and flagged as such: the three-value budget sweep, whose top-up was attempted the same day and blocked when the OpenRouter account ran out of credits mid-series - read the RANKING of the three budgets as unmeasured; the suppression claim does not depend on it. The scores, cost and wall are unchanged. EARLIER CORRECTIONS, 2026-09-11, on three counts, while adding the Qwen3.8-Flash rows. (1) HARNESS. This row was published as 'Claude Code / Alibaba API'. It never called Alibaba's API. The arm ran via=kimi_proxy2:8792 with upstream=OpenRouter's qwen3.8-max slug, so the path was Claude Code -> local proxy -> OpenRouter -> Alibaba, exactly like the Kimi K3, Ox Alpha and GLM-5.3 rows, all of which correctly say 'Claude Code / OpenRouter'. This row was the only OR-routed row on the board claiming a direct vendor API. (2) EFFORT STATUS. It was published verified_ceiling. No probe receipt exists - the only Qwen file in results/effort-dial-probes is the 2026-09-11 Flash one. The claim rested on QwenCloud's documented enum (low|medium|xhigh, default xhigh, high->xhigh) plus a check that thinking was live (248 thinking blocks across the raw logs). Under this board's own vocabulary that is first_party - a documented tier taken at face value - because verified_ceiling requires a probe that SEPARATES the levels. The row's own note also argued that Alibaba validates effort 'while OR accepts any string and applies none', which cannot both be true of a request routed through OR; whether the effort field survived the proxy and the aggregator to reach Alibaba was never established. (3) COST, $31.10 -> $33.30. The arm modelled cache writes as FREE. OpenRouter lists qwen3.8-max-0902 cache writes at $2.50/MTok and this run wrote 879,902 cache-creation tokens. A sweep of OR's listing found Qwen is the ONLY family on this board it charges a cache-write fee for - DeepSeek, Z.ai, Moonshot, Tencent and Meta publish none - so $0.00 is right on every other aggregator-routed arm and was wrong only here. The SCORES are unchanged; only the two labels and the cost move. And a caveat larger than the correction: 12.94% of this row's prompt tokens (8,282,777 of them, $16.57 - HALF the row) were billed as uncached input, against 0.002% on the two Flash rows running the same harness against Alibaba's own endpoint. That ~5,000x gap in cache-miss rate is a property of the proxy-plus-aggregator path, not of the model, so read this row's cost as a cost OF THAT PATH rather than a price for Qwen3.8-Max. NOT re-probed on purpose: the Aug 3 arm used an unlisted qwen3.8-max slug and what OpenRouter lists now is qwen3.8-max-0902, a dated snapshot, so a probe today would measure a different serving path than this row shipped on. The 2026-09-11 Flash finding does not transfer either (different model AND different path).

Tencent Hunyuan 4 preview (MoE, 49B active of 770B), benchmarked day-one via OpenRouter. 18/105 for $3.13 real OpenRouter bill. On repo 1 it claimed 10 fixes and 9 verified against the answer key. Single host (Tencent Cloud); day-one 429/404s absorbed by proxy retries. EFFORT CORRECTED 2026-09-12, from `high / first_party` to `default / inert_default`. The day-one row took Tencent's documentation at its word - reasoning_effort is a BINARY switch, `high` (the default) or `no_think`, so there is no higher tier to ask for - and published the tier the arm REQUESTED. Probing the route it actually ran on says the request never arrived: at n=3 per condition on OpenRouter's /v1/messages, both spellings overlap the no-field baseline, the baseline is the HIGHEST band of the five (mean 13,520 output tokens against 8,243 for nested high), and `bogus_zzz` returns HTTP 200 on both spellings while an invented model id 400s - no validation, so nothing downstream reads the field. Receipt: results/effort-dial-probes/20260912-hy4preview-openrouter.txt. The row is still at the model's ceiling, but for a different reason than it claimed: not because the tier was asserted and applied, but because Tencent's documented default IS the top of a two-position switch. That is a fact about Tencent's serving, not about this run - which is the whole distinction the correction makes.

runs.caveat: One run. Effort is the provider default and the aggregator hop is PROVEN inert rather than assumed: Muse Code defaults its reasoning effort to high and sends it, OpenRouter drops it, and four receipts at n=9 on this exact path show all four tiers plus no-field overlapping, with bogus_zzz returning HTTP 200 while a bad model id returns 400. Meta's own endpoint 400-rejects an invalid effort string, so the break is localised to the OpenRouter hop - the same first-party-real / aggregator-inert split already on file for Muse Spark 1.2. The route is an aggregator because Meta's own endpoint answers 402 here, billing verification failed, which is also why cost is a REAL OpenRouter credits delta rather than a list estimate. The benchmark repos were re-installed from the same lockfile inside Linux before the agent started, because the Windows install lays down win32 binaries Linux node cannot execute and an agent that cannot run the suite is solving a different task than every other row.
runs.note: The first row on this board driven by a vendor's OWN agent rather than by Claude Code. Muse Code 0.1.0 runs the loop, picks the tools and decides when to stop, and Meta's model answers it - the same experiment the Kimi CLI row runs for Moonshot. *** DO NOT READ THIS AS A HARNESS A/B AGAINST THE OTHER META ROW *** The board's only other Meta row is Muse Spark 1.2 in Claude Code, on Meta's own endpoint, at a genuine xhigh (17/105). Against this row the MODEL VERSION, the HARNESS, the ROUTE and the EFFORT all differ, so the pair is a comparison of two stacks as shipped and not an isolation of any one of them. Muse Code is chattier than a single agent loop by design: it runs a reminder-observer side-agent alongside the main one, so the turn count and the token bill both include work no Claude Code row does. *** WHY THIS ROW NEEDED TWO HARNESS FIXES BEFORE IT COULD EXIST *** Neither is a property of the model and both are disclosed because they changed what ran. First, the launcher that starts the Meta-API shim inside WSL had never once worked - it backgrounded the shim inside a session that is torn down the instant the launching shell exits, so the shim died before it could create its own log file. Second, and less visibly, the shim was not asking upstream for a stream: Muse Code requests one with an Accept header, OpenRouter reads the body, so every turn arrived as a single blob when generation finished - and Muse Code kills a run whose model stream has been idle for 180 seconds, on a route that routinely takes 200 to 230 seconds per call. The first attempt at this arm was billed for a response it never saw. Both legs of this row ran with both fixes in place.

runs.note: The second ZERO, and the more instructive of the pair, because it did not run out of anything - it decided it was finished. On repo 1 it spent 55 seconds and 18 shell calls and then reported that all the public APIs were exercised by the suite, that type checking and the tests passed, and that no bugs were located that require a code change. The prompt it was given says in as many words that a number of subtle bugs have been deliberately planted, that the suite passes anyway, and that some tests which would have caught a planted bug were neutralised when it was planted. It used a green suite as proof of a clean repo after being told that a green suite proves nothing. On repo 2 it filed a report and scored zero on it: 0 of 60, no partials, and - the one thing to its credit - zero claimed-only, so it did not invent fixes it had not made. The whole arm cost eleven cents. *** THIS IS THE THIRD ATTEMPT AT THIS ARM AND THE FIRST CLEAN ONE, WHICH THE ROW WOULD BE DISHONEST WITHOUT *** Pass 1 ran before the harness carried any context declaration. Pass 2 ran with --autocompact 100000 on it, a flag since measured INERT on both routes by two controlled pairs - so whatever pass 2 was, it was not the flag doing it. Both passes were discarded and their rows dropped before this one ran. Pass 3 carries no flag and it is mechanically clean on both legs: terminal_reason=completed, zero auto-compactions, no breaker, no truncation, no denied tool call. That matters because this board voids a leg whose ENVIRONMENT failed and scores a leg whose MODEL failed, and the runner checks the transcript to tell them apart rather than guessing from an exit code. Here it counted successful tool calls and zero permission denials on every leg. The environment was fine. *** EFFORT IS THE PROVIDER DEFAULT AND THE ROUTE IS PROBED, NOT ASSUMED *** The arm carries no --effort flag, and that is a weaker claim than it sounds: a logging pass-through measured an UNFLAGGED Claude Code putting output_config.effort=xhigh on every main call, so there is no send-nothing mode. OpenRouter does not implement output_config, so on this route the tier is dropped in transit and what runs is Groq's own default - which is what makes default honest here and would not make it honest on a first-party endpoint. Receipts: effort-dial-probes/20260912-claude-code-wire-default-effort.txt and effort-dial-probes/20260912-gptoss20b-groq-openrouter.txt. Both legs completed, the environment was verified healthy from the transcript, and the judge read a real submission on repo 2.
